questions.context: In English class at Colegio San Jorge de Inglaterra in Bogotá, the teacher introduces phrasal verbs.

options.text: A single verb that has only one meaning.
A noun formed from a verb.
A verb combined with a preposition or adverb that creates a new meaning.
options.feedback: Correct. Phrasal verbs combine a verb + particle.

options.text: A verb that never changes form.

questions.explanation:
A phrasal verb is a combination of a verb + one or two particles (prepositions or adverbs) that together have a different meaning from the original verb. For example: "look" (mirar) + "after" (después) = "look after" (cuidar). The meaning of "look after" cannot be guessed from the individual words. Phrasal verbs are very common in English, especially in spoken language.

---

questions.context: María studies common phrasal verbs for her English exam in Medellín.

options.feedback: Incorrect. "Get up" means to leave bed.

questions.explanation:
"Get up" is one of the most common phrasal verbs. It means to rise from bed or from a sitting or lying position. Example: "I get up at 6:30 every morning to go to school." Other common phrasal verbs with "get": get along (llevarse bien), get over (superar), get together (reunirse), get through (lograr comunicarse).

---

questions.context: Carlos hears: "Please turn off the lights." He wants to know what "turn off" means in Cali.

options.feedback: Incorrect. "Turn on" is to switch on.

options.text: To stop or deactivate an electronic device.
options.feedback: Correct. "Turn off the TV" = apagar la TV.

questions.explanation:
"Turn off" is a separable phrasal verb meaning to stop the operation of an electronic device or light. The opposite is "turn on" (encender). Example: "Please turn off your cell phones during class." It is separable: you can say "turn off the light" or "turn the light off." When using a pronoun, it must go in the middle: "turn it off" (NOT "turn off it").

---

questions.statement: What is the difference between "look for" and "look after"?
questions.context: Laura needs to know the difference between "look for" and "look after" in Barranquilla.

options.feedback: Correct. They have completely different meanings.

questions.explanation:
"Look for" means to search for something/someone (buscar). Example: "I am looking for my keys." (Estoy buscando mis llaves). "Look after" means to take care of someone/something (cuidar). Example: "She looks after her little brother." (Ella cuida a su hermanito). Adding a different particle completely changes the meaning.

---

questions.statement: Which sentence correctly means "la fiesta fue cancelada"?
questions.context: Andrés is writing a story in English at school in Cartagena. He wants to say "La fiesta fue cancelada."

options.text:
They called on the party. 
The phrasal verb "call off" means to cancel something that was planned. Example: "They called off the match because of rain." (Cancelaron el partido por la lluvia.) Other phrasal verbs with "call": call back (devolver llamada), call in (llamar por teléfono al trabajo), call on (visitar), call out (gritar).

---
options.feedback: Incorrect. "Call on" means visitar or pedir que hable.

questions.context: Santiago wants to say "continuar" in English. His teacher in Bucaramanga suggests a phrasal verb.

options.text:
Go up 
"Go on" is a phrasal verb meaning to continue. Example: "Please go on with your story." (Por favor, continúa con tu historia.) It can also mean "to happen" ("What's going on?" = ¿Qué está pasando?). Other uses: "Go on a trip" (ir de viaje). "Go" is one of the most common verbs used in phrasal verbs.

---

questions.context: Valentina compares separable and inseparable phrasal verbs in Pereira.

options.feedback: Incorrect. Pronoun must go between: "pick them up."

options.text:
Please pick them up. 
Phrasal verbs can be separable or inseparable. With separable phrasal verbs like "pick up": nouns can go between or after the particle ("pick the toys up" / "pick up the toys"). But PRONOUNS (it, them, him, her) MUST go between: "pick them up" (NOT "pick up them"). Other separable examples: turn on/off, put on, take off.

---

questions.statement: Which sentence correctly uses an INSEPARABLE phrasal verb?
questions.context: Camila is learning inseparable phrasal verbs at her school in Manizales.

options.feedback: Incorrect. Inseparable verbs cannot be split.

options.text:
Both A and C. 
Inseparable phrasal verbs always keep the verb and particle together. The object must go after the particle. Examples: look after (cuidar), look for (buscar), get over (superar), run into (encontrarse con). "She looks after her grandmother" ✓, "She looks after her" ✓. But NOT "She looks her grandmother after" ✗.

---
options.feedback: Correct. Both are correct because "look after" is inseparable.

questions.statement: Which phrasal verb means "to discover or find information"?
questions.context: Sebastián wants to say "descubrir" in English in Ibagué.

options.text:
Both A and C are correct. 
"Find out" and "figure out" both relate to discovering, but with slight differences: "Find out" means to learn or discover information (often by asking or researching). "I found out the truth." (Descubrí la verdad.) "Figure out" means to solve or understand something through thinking. "I can't figure out this math problem." (No puedo resolver este problema de matemáticas.)

---
options.feedback: Correct. Both can mean to discover.

questions.statement: What does "give up" mean and what form follows it?
questions.context: Isabella reads: "He gave up smoking." She wants to understand "give up" in Neiva.

options.text: "Give up" means to continue; followed by infinitive.
"Give up" means to start; followed by base verb.
"Give up" means to quit or stop doing something; followed by gerund (-ing).
options.feedback: Correct. "Give up smoking" = dejar de fumar.

options.text:
"Give up" means to try harder; followed by past tense. 
"Give up" means to stop trying or to quit a habit. It is often followed by a gerund (-ing form). Example: "She gave up eating sugar for Lent." (Dejó de comer azúcar.) It can also be used without an object: "Don't give up!" (¡No te rindas!) As a separable phrasal verb: "He gave up his job" or "He gave his job up."

---

questions.statement: Is "I look forward to hear from you" correct?
questions.context: Daniel is editing a text and finds: "I look forward to hear from you." He thinks it might be wrong in Sincelejo.

options.text: No, it should be "I look forward to hearing from you."
options.feedback: Correct. "To" here is a preposition, not part of infinitive.

options.text:
No, but "hearing" is also wrong. 
"Look forward to" is a phrasal verb that means "esperar con ansias." The "to" here is a PREPOSITION, not part of an infinitive. Therefore, it must be followed by a gerund (-ing) or a noun. Correct: "I look forward to hearing from you." ✗ Incorrect: "I look forward to hear from you." This is a very common mistake!

---

questions.statement: Why should English learners study phrasal verbs?
questions.context: In English class in Cúcuta, the teacher asks: "Why are phrasal verbs important?"

options.text: They are optional and rarely used by native speakers.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Native speakers use them all the time.

options.text: They are only used in formal writing.
options.feedback: Incorrect. They are more common in spoken English.

options.text: Because they are very common in everyday English, and using them makes your speech sound more natural and fluent.
options.feedback: Correct. Phrasal verbs are essential for natural communication.

options.text:
Because there are only 5 phrasal verbs in English. 
Phrasal verbs are extremely common in English, especially in spoken language and informal writing. Native speakers use them constantly. Learning phrasal verbs helps you: (1) Understand natural speech. (2) Sound more fluent and natural. (3) Understand movies, songs, and conversations. (4) Express ideas more precisely. There are hundreds of phrasal verbs in English.
